# Neonatal mortality among disaggregated Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander populations

**Authors:** Isabelle Nguyên Ý Maricar; Daniel Helkey; Santhosh Nadarajah; Risa Akiba; Adrian Matias Bacong; Sheila Razdan; Latha Palaniappan; Ciaran S. Phibbs; Jochen Profit

## Abstract

We compared neonatal (<28 days) mortality rates (NMRs) across disaggregated Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (AANHPI) groups using recent, national data.

We used 2015–2019 cohort-linked birth-infant death records from the National Vital Statistics System. Our sample included 61,703 neonatal deaths among 18,709,743 births across all racial and ethnic groups. We compared unadjusted NMRs across disaggregated AANHPI groups, then compared NMRs adjusting for maternal sociodemographic, maternal clinical, and neonatal risk factors.

Unadjusted NMRs differed by over 3-fold amongst disaggregated AANHPI groups. Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander neonates in aggregate had the highest fully-adjusted odds of mortality (OR: 1.08 [95% CI: 0.89, 1.31]) compared to non-Hispanic White neonates. Filipino, Asian Indian, and Other Asian neonates experienced significant decreases in odds ratios after adjusting for neonatal risk factors.

Aggregating AANHPI neonates masks large heterogeneity and undermines opportunities to provide targeted care to higher-risk groups.

## INTRODUCTION

Compared with other racial groups, Asian Americans consistently have one of the lowest neonatal mortality rates (NMRs), an important indicator of infant, child, and maternal well-being [1, 2]. In 2019, Asian Americans had the lowest NMR of 2.41 deaths per 1000 live births compared to the national rate of 3.69 per 1000 [2]. However, aggregated NMRs for Asian Americans fail to represent the large heterogeneity within this racial group. In addition, neonatal mortality research often aggregates Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (AANHPI) populations due to small sample sizes and inconsistencies in reporting of race [3–9]. This practice masks important differences between groups, preventing healthcare providers from identifying groups requiring more targeted care [8, 10].

Neonatal mortality research disaggregating AANHPI populations is limited. Previous studies use data from the early 2000s or examine specific states (namely California, which has a large AANHPI population) [11–14]. While several studies focus on individual AANHPI groups, few comprehensively explore disparities between groups [15–20]. AANHPIs as an aggregate are the fastest-growing racial and ethnic group in the US, representing more than 50 ethnicities and 100 languages [21, 22]. Therefore, updated national accounting is needed to understand the complexity of newborn health outcomes for these populations.

The objective of this study was to use recent, linked population-based national data to highlight the large heterogeneity in neonatal mortality among AANHPI neonates. We further examined differences in NMRs between ethnic groups after adjusting for maternal sociodemographic, maternal clinical, and neonatal risk factors. While we acknowledge that categorization by race and ethnicity does represent the full range of individual diversity, these groupings are important when assessing equitable care and can be clinically useful when sociocultural factors are taken into account [23].

## METHODS

### Study population

The study population was singleton infants born from 2015 to 2019 in the United States. We used the birth-cohort-linked birth and infant-death records from the National Vital Statistics System, provided by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [24]. This annual dataset provides a publicly available census of births and linked infant deaths from all 50 US states and territories [25]. We limited our analysis to data from 2015 to 2019 to focus on recent national mortality findings while avoiding potential confounding and period effects due to the COVID-19 pandemic. We restricted the data to singleton infants to ease comparative risk selection within gestational age categories and identification of small for gestational age infants. We performed a sensitivity analysis which found our results remained robust after including and adjusting for multiple births.

We classified each birth based on the self-reported race and ethnicity of the mother on the birth certificate, excluding births with unspecified maternal race or ethnicity. Previous studies have confirmed this method of race and ethnicity classification as valid [26, 27]. While not all birthing persons identify as mothers, we used the term “mother” to reflect the language used in our dataset. We included the following categorization of non-Hispanic Asian American ethnicities: Asian Indian, Chinese, Filipino, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, and Other Asian. “Other Asian” neonates include any other recorded Asian American ethnicity. Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander (NH/PI) neonates were initially disaggregated when calculating mortality rates (Hawaiian, Samoan, Guamanian, and “Other Pacific Islander”) but were later combined in our multivariable analysis due to small sample sizes for individual groups. We selected non-Hispanic White (NHW) neonates, the most populous group of infants in our study, as our reference group. Additionally, we included all non-AANHPI groups (non-Hispanic Black, American Indian/Alaskan Native, Hispanic, and multiple-race neonates) to support our comparative analyses.

### Variables

Our primary outcome was neonatal mortality, defined as death within 28 days of birth. We used risk adjustment to account for various maternal sociodemographic, maternal clinical, and neonatal clinical factors. Maternal sociodemographic risk factors included maternal age (<18, 18–34, or >34 years), marital status (married or single) [28], nativity (US-born or foreign-born) [29], insurance status (Medicaid, private insurance, self-pay, or other insurance types) [30], and education (<high school, high school/General Educational Development diploma, college with no degree, Associate degree, Bachelor’s degree, or graduate degree). Maternal clinical risk factors included delivery type (vaginal or Cesarean section), smoking during pregnancy, number of prior births (0, 1–3, or >3), number of prior terminations (including spontaneous or induced abortions or ectopic pregnancies) (0, 1–3, or >3), pre-pregnancy or gestational diabetes, pre-pregnancy or gestational hypertension, preeclampsia and eclampsia, and prenatal care during any trimester of pregnancy. Neonatal clinical factors included neonatal sex, gestational age in weeks, and low birth weight for gestational age [31]. We accounted for missing values or values recorded as missing in each risk factor by constructing a “missing” category. All risk factors were recorded as categorical or indicator variables.

### Statistical analysis

NMRs were computed for each racial and ethnic group as the number of deaths per 1000 live births. We used the recorded weight to adjust for unlinked death records when comparing NMRs. We used an iterative approach to risk adjust for differences in case-mix, using multivariate logistic regression models to compare NMRs across all groups. Indicator variables representing each racial and ethnic group were used in logistic regression models to compare each group’s mortality with the reference group of NHW neonates. We used the resulting coefficient estimates to construct point estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for odds ratios (ORs).

We summarized frequency and distribution of all descriptive variables (Tables). To identify differences in mortality, we first computed unadjusted NMRs for each racial and ethnic group (Model 1). Second, we adjusted for maternal sociodemographic and maternal clinical factors (Model 2). Lastly, we applied a model with all risk factors (i.e., maternal sociodemographic and maternal clinical risk factors combined with neonatal factors) (Model 3). We also tested an incremental model including maternal sociodemographic and maternal clinical risk factors separately, but this model performed nearly identically to the combined maternal risk factor model, and so was not included in the final analysis (results available in Supplementary Table 1). Neonatal characteristics were adjusted last to illustrate the contributions of low birth weight and low gestational age, both of which are highly associated with neonatal mortality. Data was processed with SAS software, using data importing code from the National Center for Health Statistics [32–35]. Statistical tests were implemented in Python 3.9.13 using statsmodels 0.13.2 [32, 33]. All code and processing were performed on a secure server at the Stanford University School of Medicine.

## RESULTS

Our analysis included 18,709,743 births, of which 6.8% were AANHPI neonates (1,264,991) compared to 52.2% for NHW (9,766,379). Asian Indian, Chinese, and Other Asians were the three largest groups (Table 1), comprising 28.3%, 22.4%, and 17.8% of all AANHPI births, respectively. The smallest groups among AANHPI births were NH/PI (3.9%) and Japanese (2.4%). AANHPI neonates in aggregate accounted for ~5% of all neonatal deaths, with an unadjusted NMR of 2.4 deaths per 1000 births. Disaggregated unadjusted NMRs varied by over 3-fold, ranging from 1.4 per 1000 births among Chinese neonates to 4.9 per 1000 births among Samoans (see Supplementary Table 2 for all disaggregated NMR values). When compared with all other racial and ethnic groups, Samoan neonates had the second highest unadjusted NMR below non-Hispanic Black neonates (4.9 vs 6.3).

### Risk factors

Tables 1, 2, and 3 summarize the variability of maternal sociodemographic, maternal clinical, and neonatal risk factors by race and ethnicity (descriptive data for risk factors for disaggregated NH/PI groups and non-AANHPI groups can be found in Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Most AANHPI mothers were foreign-born (80.0%) and married (71.4%) (Table 1). However, nativity varied widely, with around 10.4% of Asian Indian mothers born in the U.S. compared to around 28% for Japanese, Filipino, and Other Asian, and more than 35% for NH/PI mothers. More than 27% of aggregated AANHPI mothers were greater than 34 years of age compared to NHW mothers (<18%). Japanese mothers had the largest proportion of births over 34 years of age (49.1%). 45% of Other Asian and 52.2% of NH/PI mothers were Medicaid-insured. Over 66% of Chinese and Japanese mothers and more than 77% of Asian Indian and Korean mothers held Bachelor’s or advanced degrees, compared to roughly 41.1% of Vietnamese and 38.1% of Other Asian mothers. Notably, more than half of NH/PI mothers had either a high school education or less.

There was also large variation across AANHPI groups for maternal clinical risk factors (Table 2). Close to 15% of Asian Indian mothers had pre-pregnancy or gestational diabetes, compared to roughly 7.4% for Japanese mothers and 6.3% for NHW mothers. More than 9% of Filipino mothers had pre-pregnancy or gestational hypertension, compared to less than 3% among Chinese mothers. Among all AANHPI groups, NH/PI mothers reported the highest percentage of cigarette use during pregnancy (4.1%) and more than three prior births (14.0%), compared to Asian Indian mothers who reported the lowest percentage of cigarette use during pregnancy (0.1%) and Chinese mothers who reported the lowest percentage of more than three prior births (0.6%). NH/PI mothers also had the highest percentage of no prenatal care (4.7%) compared to Chinese mothers (0.5%). When examining neonatal risk factors (Table 3), more than 21% of Filipino and NH/PI neonates in aggregate were born prematurely (gestational age <37 weeks), compared to roughly 12.2% of Chinese neonates. Around 8.5% of Asian Indian and Filipino neonates had birth weights less than 2500 g, compared to only 4.4% of Chinese neonates.

### Adjusted mortality

Figure 1 shows the differences in neonatal mortality after adjusting for the selected risk factors. Each racial and ethnic group shows a set of ORs and 95% CIs for different adjustment models. ORs for our regression models reflect differences in mortality compared to NHW neonates. For both unadjusted (Model 1) and fully-adjusted models (Model 3), AANHPI neonates in aggregate had lower likelihoods of mortality compared to NHW neonates (OR [95% CI]; 0.90 [0.86, 0.93], 0.84 [0.79, 0.89]). However, both unadjusted and adjusted mortality varied significantly across disaggregated groups.

Chinese, Japanese, and Korean neonates had significantly lower likelihoods of mortality both before and after adjusting for maternal and neonatal risk factors compared to NHW neonates (OR [95% CI] before and after risk adjustment, Chinese: 0.53 [0.48, 0.58], 0.68 [0.59, 0.78]; Japanese: 0.56 [0.42, 0.74], 0.65 [0.44, 0.96]; Korean: 0.61 [0.51, 0.73], 0.67 [0.52, 0.86]). These groups also had the lowest ORs among all AANHPI neonates and other racial groups, though these results were not all statistically significant. In contrast, Asian Indian, Filipino, and Other Asian neonates had significantly increased odds of mortality after adjusting for maternal sociodemographic and maternal clinical factors (Model 2) but had decreased odds after accounting for neonatal risk factors (Asian Indian: 1.38 [1.28, 1.50], 0.82 [0.75, 0.89]; Filipino: 1.30 [1.15, 1.47], 0.85 [0.75, 0.98]; Other Asian: 1.35 [1.24, 1.48], 0.89 [0.80, 0.99]).

Compared to NHW neonates, NH/PI neonates in aggregate experienced increased odds of mortality in unadjusted analyses (1.64 [1.43, 1.87]). ORs remained stable after first adjusting for maternal risk factors (Model 2, 1.59 [1.35, 1.87]) but decreased after adjusting for neonatal risk factors (Model 3, 1.08 [0.89, 1.31]).

## DISCUSSION

We found considerable heterogeneity in neonatal mortality across AANHPI groups by over 3-fold. Overall, our results suggest AANHPI neonates have population-specific maternal, pregnancy, and neonatal risk profiles, resulting in divergent neonatal mortality.

Our results extend and update a study by Baker et al. which examined disaggregated AANHPI neonatal mortality trends using California data from 1991 to 2001 [12]. We note that in the time between the years analyzed in Baker et al. and our study, AANHPI populations have grown exponentially, including the percentage of U.S.-born women [36]. We similarly found that after adjusting for maternal sociodemographic, maternal clinical, and neonatal risk factors, Filipino neonates experienced 15% decreased odds of mortality compared to NHW neonates. In addition, we found that Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese neonates showed no significant changes in mortality rate after adjusting for maternal and neonatal risk factors. However, in contrast to Baker et al. who found that Chinese neonates had similarly adjusted NMRs as NHW neonates, we showed that Chinese neonates experienced lower unadjusted and adjusted mortality [12]. We also found that risk-adjusted mortality for Asian Indian neonates was significantly lower after adjusting for maternal and neonatal risk factors compared to NHW neonates, while Baker et al. found that mortality for Asian Indian neonates was similar to NHW neonates.

When comparing all racial and ethnic groups in our analysis, NH/PI neonates in aggregate had the highest fully-adjusted mortality rate, followed closely by American Indian/Alaskan Native neonates. Despite a higher prevalence of maternal risk factors, NH/PI neonatal mortality remained relatively stable after first adjusting for maternal risk factors (see Fig. 1). However, compared to other AANHPI groups, NH/PI neonates experienced the second-largest decrease in mortality odds after adjusting for neonatal risk factors (below Asian Indian neonates). This may reflect our findings in Table 3, which show that around 19% of NH/PI neonates had a gestational age less than 37 weeks and 16.8% had birth weights outside normal ranges (<2500 or ≥4000 g). A scoping review on NH/PI maternal and infant health outcomes highlighted a similar high prevalence of preterm births and risk factors [37].

Asian Indian, Filipino, and Other Asian neonates also had a significant decrease in mortality rate after adjusting for neonatal risk factors. This finding may reflect the higher prevalences of low gestational age and out-of-range birth weight we found among these groups compared to Chinese, Korean, and Japanese mothers as found in other studies [38, 39]. A study linking California hospital births from 2007 to 2018 found that compared to other AANHPI groups, Filipino, Cambodian, Laotian, and NH/PI mothers were at increased risk for pregnancy-related conditions and perinatal outcomes, including preterm birth and very low birth weight [38]. Studies have also found that infants born to Asian Indian mothers were at higher risk of being small for gestational age compared to other Asian American groups [38, 39]. In addition, our finding among Asian Indian, Filipino, and Other Asian neonates may also reflect individual maternal socioeconomic and clinical risk factors we adjusted for that were grouped in our analysis. For example, Asian Indian (14.7%) and Filipino (13.4%) mothers had the highest proportions with pre-pregnancy or gestational diabetes compared to Japanese mothers (7.4%). These variations in maternal risk are similar to findings from perinatal outcomes studies using only California health records data [38, 40]. Future studies should further investigate the unique risk profiles among AANHPI neonates with special attention to the impacts of low gestational age and low birth weight on mortality.

This study has some limitations. First, sample sizes were small for some groups, particularly for NH/PI neonates, who were aggregated in our final analysis. While this may be due to the limited years we chose to include in our study (2015–2019) and potential reporting bias from mothers, small sample sizes could also be due to the categorization of race and ethnicity. Neonates whose mothers identified as multiple-race may also identify as multiple-race AANHPI, however, for our analysis, they were analyzed separately under the category “Multiple Race”. According to the 2020 Census, 4.1 million people identified as Asian in combination with another race, and nearly 900,000 people identified as NH/PI in combination with another race [41]. Second, results for Other Asian and Other PI neonates are difficult to interpret as they mask other AANHPI groups. While other datasets, such as the California Vitals Statistics Records, may provide more granular data on specific Asian American groups (such as Cambodian, Thai, and Laotian neonates), the National Vital Statistics System only provides data on the six largest groups. Third, similar to AANHPI neonates, Hispanic neonates are not a homogenous group, and our lack of disaggregating this group is a limitation to our comparative analysis. Lastly, our study relied on vital statistics data based on linked birth and death certificates. While we were able to adjust for several risk factors associated with neonatal mortality, other confounding factors, such as acculturation and reliable congenital anomaly diagnoses, were unavailable or unreliable [42, 43]. Several maternal risk factors, including smoking during pregnancy, prenatal care, gestational diabetes and hypertension, and pregnancy complications, are known to be of poor quality and low sensitivity [43–45]. There is significant missing data for maternal marital status (Table 1), as California, the residence of nearly one-third of AANHPI mothers, does not report marital status after 2017 [46]. Leveraging and linking other more accurate data sources on culture, behaviors, or other social determinants of health may provide further insight into the unique risk profiles of AANHPI neonates.

## CONCLUSION

Our work highlights the substantial heterogeneity in neonatal mortality among AANHPI groups using recent, national data. Treating AANHPI populations as a homogenous group masks significant variation and prevents opportunities to improve neonatal outcomes. Investigating the contribution of risk factors among groups with decreased odds of mortality can provide opportunities to improve outcomes among other groups at higher risk. The aggregation bias can be extended to explore disparities among other racial and ethnic groups (e.g., Hispanic neonates). Future work using disaggregated group classifications and sufficient sample sizes should be done to target inequities in AANHPI maternal and neonatal health.

## Abstract

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevalence varies widely among Asian American adults. The American Heart Association added healthy sleep to its metrics to define ideal cardiovascular health. Little is known about the association between sleep and CVD prevalence among Asian subgroups. We aim to examine the association between suboptimal sleep duration and CVD risk prevalence among Asian American subgroups.

We used 2012 to 2018 National Health Interview Survey data to examine the association between suboptimal sleep duration and CVD prevalence. We included 6868 self‐identifying Asian adults age >40 years (Asian Indian [n=1053], Chinese [n=1415], Filipino [n=1734], and Other Asian [n=2666] adults). Suboptimal sleep was defined as <7 or >9 hours per night. CVD was defined as self‐reported stroke, heart attack, coronary artery disease, or angina. Logistic regression was used to calculate odds ratios and 95% CI to estimate the association between suboptimal sleep duration and CVD prevalence. Filipino and Other Asian participants with suboptimal sleep had the highest prevalence of CVD. Aggregated Asian American participants with suboptimal sleep duration had a higher prevalence of CVD (odds ratio [95% CI, 1.35 [1.09–1.68]) compared with those with optimal sleep duration. After stratification by race or ethnicity or both, a significant association persisted for Other Asian participants (1.77 [95% CI, 1.27–2.46]) but not among all other Asian American subgroups.

Our study highlights the heterogeneity of CVD prevalence associated with suboptimal sleep duration among Asian American adults. Future studies should consider how different measures of sleep duration and quality affect CVD outcomes among disaggregated Asian American subgroups.

## What Is New?

- Suboptimal sleep duration is associated with higher cardiovascular disease prevalence in Other Asian adults, but not Chinese, Indian, or Filipino adults.

- Other Asian adults with suboptimal sleep duration have 40% higher odds of cardiovascular disease compared with their counterparts with optimal sleep duration.

## What Are the Clinical Implications?

- Asian American adults should be screened for sleep duration as part of comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment.

In 2022, the American Heart Association recognized sleep health as a cardiovascular risk factor as part of the “Life's Essential Eight,” which previously included blood lipids, blood glucose, blood pressure, diet, physical activity, nicotine exposure, and body mass index (BMI). 1 Poor sleep health increases cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk and is associated with hypertension, diabetes, depression, and impaired cognition. 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 Optimal sleep duration varies by age group but the American Heart Association recommends that adults obtain between 7 and 9 hours of sleep daily for optimal cardiovascular health. 6 Sleep duration affects cognition, diabetes, and cardiometabolic health, and poor sleep duration is associated with higher mortality. 7 , 8 , 9 , 10

Sleep duration is not well studied within Asian American subgroups, because most research examines sleep duration in non‐Hispanic Whites and Asian Americans in aggregate due to small sample size. 11 While many cardiovascular risk factors and health outcomes vary between Asian American subgroups, the availability of disaggregated Asian American health information is limited to a few national data sets, including the National Health Interview Study (NHIS). 12 , 13 , 14

Few studies have used national surveys to examine the association between sleep duration and CVD risk and prevalence in Asian American adults. 15 , 16 These studies combined Asian American adults into “Other persons” or “Other minorities” categories. These classifications often include Pacific Islander adults, multiracial persons, and any other racial or ethnic group whose numbers are too low to identify. Asian‐American adults are a highly heterogeneous population, especially with respect to CVD prevalence and risk factors. Asian‐America adults of South Asian origin are at higher risk of developing CVD compared with other Asian subgroups; therefore, aggregation can mask significant differences among this racial group. 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21

In this study, we examine the association between sleep health and CVD among disaggregated Asian‐American subgroups. We hypothesize that the association of poor sleep and CVD prevalence will vary significantly by Asian‐American subgroups.

## METHODS

### Study Population

We analyzed data from the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), an annual cross‐sectional, complex survey conducted among representative households of the noninstitutionalized US population. 22 The NHIS was approved by the National Center for Health Statistics Internal Review Board and received informed consent from all respondents. All data have been made publicly available by the National Center for Health Statistics and can be accessed at https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/data‐questionnaires‐documentation.htm.

Survey structure and data collection are described in detail elsewhere. 23 We limited our analysis to the years 2012 to 2018 due to inconsistent reporting of cardiovascular risk factors before 2012. Our sample of 6868 participants included Asian Indian participants (n=1053), Chinese participants (n=1415), Filipino participants (n=1734), and Other Asian participants (n=2666) over the age of 40 years (lower age groups were excluded due to low CVD prevalence). Other Asian participants included Korean, Japanese, and Vietnamese American participants as well as additional unspecified Asian American subgroups, Native Hawaiian participants, and Pacific Islander participants. Race and ethnicity were self‐reported, and all Asian participants were the reference group. Asian American survey participants with missing data on sleep duration or CVD were excluded from the analysis (n=12 302).

### Sleep Health and Duration

Sleep duration was self‐reported from the following survey question: “On average, how many hours of sleep do you get in a 24‐hour period?” Sleep was categorized based on American Heart Association definitions 1 , 8 as 7 to 9 hours per night (optimal), <7 hours per night, or >9 hours per night. Sleep duration was also dichotomized as <7 or >9 hours per night (suboptimal) or 7 to 9 hours per night (optimal).

### Cardiovascular Disease

CVD prevalence was self‐reported from the following survey questions: “Have you ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had angina, also called angina pectoris?”, “Have you ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had coronary heart disease?”, “Have you ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had a heart attack (also called myocardial infarction)?”, or “Have you ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had a stroke?” CVD prevalence was defined by an affirmative response (“yes”) to any of these questions.

### Covariates

Sociodemographic factors, all of which were self‐reported, included age, sex (male versus female), nativity (US‐born versus foreign‐born), educational level (≤high school degree/GED versus >high school degree), insurance status (public, private, versus uninsured), and annual household income ($0–$34 999, $35 000–$74 999, $75 000–$99 999, versus ≥$100 000). Nativity was dichotomized into US‐born or foreign‐born (participants born outside of the United States or US territory). Education was assessed based on the highest level of completed school or degree reported by participants. For insurance status, participants with Medicaid, Medicare, state‐sponsored health plans, or military health insurance were categorized as having public insurance. Participants who reported having private insurance or not having any insurance were grouped accordingly.

Cardiovascular risk factors included tobacco use (current/former tobacco user versus never tobacco user), alcohol use (current, former, versus never alcohol user), BMI (normal versus abnormal range), weekly moderate physical activity (sufficient versus insufficient), hypertension, high cholesterol, and diabetes. For tobacco use, participants who smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their entire life and reported smoking frequency (if applicable) were “current/former tobacco users”; otherwise, they were classified as “never tobacco users.” 24 Nontobacco nicotine exposure was excluded due to lack of data. 22 Participants who consumed ≥12 alcoholic beverages in any year or their entire life and 1 or more beverages in the past year they were surveyed were “current alcohol users”; participants who consumed ≥12 alcoholic beverages in any year or their entire life but none in the past year they were surveyed were “former alcohol users”; participants who consumed <12 alcoholic beverages in their entire life were “never alcohol users.” 25 Based on World Health Organization guidelines, normal BMI was ≤24.9 and ≥18.5 for non‐Hispanic Whites and ≤22.9 and ≥18.5 for Asian Americans; BMI outside of the respective ranges was considered abnormal. 26 Sufficient physical activity was defined as ≥150 minutes per week of moderate‐intensity aerobic physical activity, ≥75 minutes per week of vigorous‐intensity aerobic physical activity, or ≥150 minutes per week of both moderate and vigorous‐intensity aerobic physical activity; insufficient physical activity fell outside of these thresholds. 27 Self‐reported binary responses (“yes”/“no”) were used to assess hypertension, high cholesterol, and diabetes. In addition to cardiovascular risk factors consistent with American Heart Association “Life's Essential Eight,” depression was included due to its association with both sleep duration and CVD. 1 , 10 , 28

### Statistical Analysis

Sociodemographic characteristics and cardiovascular risk profiles were described using proportions, means (for age), and corresponding 95% CIs for all participants in our sample. The distribution of sleep duration categories was presented among all Asian participants and according to Asian subgroup. We used a χ2 test to determine whether sleep duration distribution differed by Asian subgroup. Next, we estimated the prevalence of CVD by dichotomous suboptimal sleep duration according to Asian subgroup race or ethnicity, using χ2 tests to test for differences. Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between dichotomous suboptimal sleep duration with CVD prevalence, with adjustments for age and sociodemographic factors (sex, nativity, education, insurance status, and income). In a sensitivity analysis we presented the association between sleep duration category (with optimal sleep duration as the reference) and CVD. In a sensitivity analysis, we additionally adjusted for cardiovascular risk factors that may mediate the association between suboptimal sleep with CVD; these include: tobacco use, alcohol use, BMI, physical activity, hypertension, high cholesterol, diabetes, and depression. All data were analyzed using appropriate complex survey design variables and weights using SUDAAN V (11.4.0).

## RESULTS

### Study Demographics

Using NHIS data from 2012 to 2018, the study included a total of 6868 (unweighted) participants representing >2.7 million Asian American adults >40 years old; 19.0% were Asian Indian participants, 22.1% were Chinese participants, 23.6% were Filipino participants, and 35.3% were Other Asian participants (Table). Other Asian participants had higher proportions of adverse socioeconomic risk factors compared with Asian Indian, Chinese, or Filipino participants. More than 35% of Other Asian participants had a high school education or less, compared with 20% of Asian Indian participants. Similarly, Other Asian participants had the highest percentages of public insurance (33.7%) or uninsured status (9.7%) compared with other Asian Indian, Chinese, or Filipino participants. Also, 30.2% of Other Asian participants had incomes <$35 000 compared with 15.6% of Asian Indian participants, who had the highest proportion of incomes >$100 000 (46.2%).

### Prevalence of Cardiovascular Disease by Sleep Duration and Race or Ethnicity

The prevalence of CVD was 8.1% (95% CI, 7.4–8.9) among all Asian participants, 7.4% (95% CI, 5.8–9.3) among Asian Indian participants, 5.7% (95% CI, 4.4–7.5) among Chinese participants, 10.7% (95% CI, 9.1–12.7) among Filipino participants, and 8.3% (95% CI, 7.2–9.5) among Other Asian participants. For All Asian participants, the prevalence of CVD was higher among those with suboptimal (10.1%) compared with optimal (6.9%) sleep duration (P <0.01, [Figure 2]). The prevalence of CVD was also higher comparing suboptimal to optimal sleep duration among Other Asian (P <0.01) but not among Asian Indian (8.1% versus 7.1%, P=0.55), Chinese (6.9% versus 5.2%, P=0.25) or Filipino (12.3% versus 9.5%, P=0.12) participants, respectively.

### Association Between Suboptimal Sleep and CVD Prevalence by Race or Ethnicity

The associations between suboptimal sleep and CVD by race or ethnicity are shown in Figure 3. After adjusting for covariates including age, sociodemographic factors, aggregated Asian American participants with suboptimal sleep duration had higher odds of CVD (odds ratio [95% CI, 1.35 [1.09–1.68]) compared with participants with optimal sleep duration. Other Asian participants had significantly higher odds of CVD with suboptimal sleep compared with optimal sleep (1.77 [95% CI, 1.27–2.46]). However, the odds ratios were not significant among Asian Indian, Chinese, or Filipino participants. Table S1 shows that compared with optimal sleep duration, only sleep duration <7 hours is associated with higher odds of CVD among All Asian participants: (1.41 [95% CI, 1.13–1.76]) and Other Asian participants: (1.96 [95% CI, 1.39–2.77]). In an additional sensitivity analysis (Table S2), adjusting for potential mediators (cardiovascular disease risk factors), optimal compared with suboptimal sleep was no longer associated with higher odds of CVD among All Asian participants: (1.15 [95% CI, 0.92–1.44]) but was still significantly associated with CVD among Other Asian participants: (1.51 [95% CI, 1.08–2.10]).

## DISCUSSION

Among all Asian American participants, individuals with suboptimal sleep had 35% higher odds of CVD compared with those with optimal sleep. After stratifying by Asian subgroup, we found that Other Asian participants had 77% higher odds of CVD with suboptimal sleep compared with those with optimal sleep. The relationship between sleep and CVD was not statistically significant among the other Asian American subgroups included in our study.

Other Asians participants were more likely to have lower education attainment, lower income, and a higher proportion of public insurance. The Filipino participants had a higher prevalence of alcohol users and self‐reported history of hypertension and high cholesterol. Our study found the strongest association with Other Asian participants, but due to the lack of specific ethnic information, it is difficult to interpret these findings with respect to which subgroups in this category have the strongest association with CVD prevalence. Some studies have specifically analyzed cardiovascular risk factors among Filipino Americans, but these are very limited. 29 , 30

Previous studies exploring sleep disparities in Asian American adults using NHIS data have found that Filipino participants were less likely to report sufficient sleep duration compared with Chinese and Asian Indian participants, which is consistent with our study findings. 31 , 32 A comprehensive review on sleep disparities among Asian American adults also found that South and Southeast Asian American adults (including Asian Indian and Filipino participants) report more poor sleep duration compared with their East Asian counterparts. 33 The higher proportions of suboptimal sleep duration among Filipino participants may be attributed to within‐group disparities in socioeconomic status, nativity, and cardiovascular risk factors among Asian American adults. 30 , 34

There are few studies that compare the association between unhealthy sleep and CVD prevalence across multiple Asian American subgroups. The limited analyses that focused on specific Asian American and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander subgroups or on populations in Asia demonstrate similar results to our findings regarding Other Asian participants. 35 , 36 , 37 For example, a recent study looking at sleep duration and chronic disease among older Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander people found that both short (≤6 hours) and long (≥9 hours) sleep duration were significantly associated with higher stroke prevalence. 35 Another study using Korean National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data from 2007 to 2010 found that short sleep duration (≤5 hours) was significantly associated with higher prevalence of stroke and ischemic heart disease among Korean participants. 36 In our study, Other Asian participants from NHIS aggregate 3 of the 6 largest Asian American subgroups (Vietnamese, Japanese, and Korean) as well as other Asian subgroups and Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander people. Although we found a significant association between suboptimal sleep and CVD prevalence among Other Asian participants, future research is needed to better understand which specific subgroups contribute to this association.

The few studies focused on Chinese, Filipino, and Asian Indian populations that were conducted in Asia found significant associations between suboptimal sleep and CVD prevalence. 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 The majority of these sleep health studies have considered sleep quality in their analyses. Sleep quality, which considers disturbances in sleep and depth of sleep, has been associated with CVD. 42 , 43 , 44 A retrospective study in India found that poor sleep quality (measured using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) was associated with a 5‐fold greater odds of coronary heart disease compared with short sleep duration alone (defined as total sleep time in hours, with total sleep time in hours not exceeding 6 hours). 41 Assessment of sleep quality (in addition to optimal sleep duration) may reveal differences in CVD prevalence among Asian American subgroups.

This study has several limitations. Small sample sizes reduced the statistical power for this analysis and did not permit disaggregation of some Asian American subgroups including Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese participants. Since NHIS is only conducted in English and Spanish, many non‐English/non‐Spanish‐speaking Asian American participants were excluded. Furthermore, our study was limited to 2012 to 2018 survey years due to missing data on race or ethnicity and major CVD risk factors outside of these years. Small sample sizes may have contributed to the lack of association between sleep duration and CVD prevalence observed among Indian, Chinese, and Filipino participants. In addition, all variables are self‐reported and therefore subject to social desirability and recall bias, potentially confounding the results. This study does not consider sleep quality because there is a lack of disaggregated sleep data in Asian American adults. Future studies will require utilizing additional data sets to not only increase Asian American sample sizes studied but also to include other means of measuring sleep duration, sleep quality, and covariates. The National Institutes of Health recently announced a new epidemiological cohort study among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander adults. 45 While this study will take time to generate prospective outcome data, it demonstrates the recognition that there is a strong need to increase research on Asian American health care outcomes. 43

## CONCLUSIONS

Our study demonstrates that significant heterogeneity exists among Asian American subgroups in the association between suboptimal sleep and CVD prevalence. These findings highlight the need for more scientific investigations to better understand the association between sleep and CVD among disaggregated Asian American subgroups. Future studies should consider how different measures of sleep duration (ie, “short” versus “long” sleep) and sleep quality may affect CVD outcomes among Asian American subgroups. Our study not only highlights the importance of data disaggregation but also demonstrates potential public health interventions focused on sleep improvement to reduce the burden of CVD among Asian American populations.

## Abstract

We examined total opioid consumption during hospitalisation across manual (MA-THA), computer-assisted (CA-THA), and robotic-assisted (RA-THA) total hip arthroplasty.

This retrospective cohort study (2016–2023, Premier Healthcare database) of patients undergoing unilateral elective THA assessed opioid consumption during hospitalisation and by postoperative day (POD). Two-part mixed-effects models were conducted: first of a logistic regression for opioid use (yes/no) and second a linear regression model of log(opioid consumption) among opioid consumers.

During hospitalisation of 584 578 patients, CA-THA was associated with lower odds of any opioid consumption than MA-THA (odds ratio [OR], 0.87; 95% confidence interval [95% CI], 0.80–0.95). RA-THA was associated with higher odds of any opioid consumption than CA-THA (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.08–1.39). Among opioid consumers, CA-THA and RA-THA were associated with a 2% lower total opioid consumption than MA-THA (both multiplicative effects [ME], 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97–0.99). The strongest effect was observed on POD 1: lower odds of opioid consumption for both CA-THA (OR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.74–0.83) and RA-THA (OR, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.80–0.88) than for MA-THA, and among those who consumed opioids, there was 9% lower (ME, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.90–0.93) and 6% lower (ME, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.93–0.96) opioid consumption for CA-THA and RA-THA, respectively, than for MA-THA.

Among those who consumed opioids, technology-assisted THA was associated with lower opioid consumption than MA-THA, primarily due to differences observed on POD 1. Although these differences are not clinically significant enough to affect decision-making, technology-assisted THA might be associated with anaesthetic techniques that confer improved pain relief in the immediate postoperative period.

Pain management is a key component of perioperative care as acute postoperative pain is directly associated with acute postoperative opioid consumption, which in turn is one of the most important independent predictors of developing chronic pain and chronic opioid use disorder.1 In the setting of total hip arthroplasty (THA), acute pain management might also have a more functional dimension, as it has been described to trigger a ‘chain reaction’ of improved short-term, and therefore long-term, functionality, patient satisfaction, and the overall patient experience post-THA.2, 3, 4

The volume of robotic-assisted (RA-THA) and computer-assisted (CA-THA) THA has increased relative to manual THA (MA-THA) over the past several years.5 The former two have been described to improve several radiological parameters measuring accuracy of component placement.6 Given this shift in practice, a relatively unexplored factor that may potentially impact perioperative pain and opioid use among THA recipients is the use of technology.

Existing studies support the idea that RA-THA leads to less opioid consumption during hospitalisation than MA-THA, whereas one study supports the same finding for CA-THA compared with MA-THA for postoperative day 1 (POD 1).5,7,8 To the best of our knowledge, no direct comparison has been made between CA-THA and RA-THA. In the face of increased use and constant evolution of technology-assisted THA, using a multi-institutional, multi-year database with recent data could provide a more accurate understanding of how surgical modality might affect opioid requirements.

Therefore, using a national US database, we aimed to examine opioid consumption during hospitalisation across MA-THA, CA-THA, and RA-THA. We hypothesised that RA-THA and CA-THA would be associated with less opioid consumption during hospitalisation compared with MA-THA.

## Methods

### Study design and setting

This retrospective cohort study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB #2012-050) at the senior author’s institution and followed the STROBE guidelines.9 The Premier Healthcare claims dataset (Premier Healthcare Solutions, Inc., Charlotte, NC, USA) was queried. It includes International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10 CM) and Procedure Codes (ICD-10 PCS), Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes, and standardised billing information for >25% of US healthcare.10

### Participants

All adults (18 yr or older) undergoing primary elective unilateral THA during 2016–2023 were assessed for eligibility. We excluded patients with missing demographic information or undergoing simultaneous bilateral THA or THA for neoplasm, fracture, or trauma. Cases with concomitant removal of hardware or conversion arthroplasties were also excluded. To ensure normality of outcome data distribution, we excluded patients with opioid consumption above the cohort’s 95th percentile11 and those treated at hospitals performing fewer than 50 THA cases per year.12

### Variables

The exposure of interest was surgical modality (MA-THA, CA-THA, and RA-THA) and three comparison groups were formed. Baseline patient characteristics collected were sex, age, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index Group (ECIG), race, ethnicity, insurance type, discharge status and year. We also documented history of neuropathic pain syndrome, complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), chronic pain (syndrome or other), fibromyalgia, or psychiatric conditions (depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder, bipolar disorder, personality disorder). Hospital characteristics collected were location (urban, rural), teaching status, size (large=500+ beds, medium=300–499 beds, small=0–299 beds), and region. Perioperative/postoperative variables retrieved were surgical indication, procedural setting (inpatient/outpatient), anaesthesia type, surgical duration, and length of stay (LOS). Because orthopaedic complications could affect opioid requirements,13 we collected periprosthetic fracture, dislocation, or other. In similar fashion, non-orthopaedic perioperative complications collected were myocardial infarction (MI), pulmonary embolism (PE), acute kidney injury (AKI), delirium, stroke, and mortality. Multimodal analgesia use, hospital, and surgeon were retrieved and used as adjustments in regression models.

The primary outcome was total opioid consumption during hospitalisation. Secondary outcomes were total opioid consumption during the day of surgery (DOS), POD 1, and on and after postoperative day 2 until discharge (POD ≥2). We opted to cluster POD ≥2 as previous analyses have shown that 2 days are the 75th percentile of LOS for THA patients.14

### Data sources/measurements

CA-THA and RA-THA were defined by extracting patients with their respective ICD-10 PCS and CPT codes from the whole THA cohort. If a surgical event included both RA-THA and CA-THA codes, it was classified as RA-THA.15 As there is no specific code for MA-THA, the procedure was considered MA-THA if it was not associated with a RA-THA or CA-THA code. ICD-10 CM codes were also used to retrieve perioperative orthopaedic and non-orthopaedic complications. A full list of the ICD-10 and CPT codes used is available in Supplementary Table 1. Anaesthesia type was defined by billing information. Similarly, multimodal analgesia use was extracted using billing information for non-opioid agents we have previously defined.16 As an adjustment in models, multimodal analgesia was used as a categorical variable: 0–1, 2, or 3+ components.17 Duration of surgery was calculated using standard procedure duration billings adjusted by a multiplier to account for deviations from billed time. Opioid consumption was extracted using billing information for opioid medication used. It was then converted and measured in morphine milligram equivalents (MME) using conversion factors.

### Statistical analysis

Categorical variables were reported as N/n and percentage and continuous variables as medians and interquartile ranges. Given the large sample size, group differences were assessed by calculating absolute standardised mean differences (SMDs), and an absolute SMD >0.1 was considered notable. Three-group SMD values were calculated using the ‘tableone’ package in R version 4.4.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) which takes the average of all pairwise SMDs when more than two groups are being compared. For opioid consumption across timepoints, we reported means and standard deviations, and medians and interquartile ranges. To measure associations between the interventions and outcomes of interest, mixed-effects models were conducted in pairwise fashion. Normality of opioid consumption was seen by Q-Q plots, and the distribution was determined to be non-normal. We handled non-normality of the opioid consumption variables by (1) removing all patients with total opioid consumption greater than the 95th percentile (540 MME)18 and (2) conducting a two-part hurdle model to manage the substantial proportion of zero values at all timepoints.19,20 The two-part model consisted first of a logistic regression which modelled the binary outcome of any opioid consumption (yes/no). The second part was a linear regression model of log(opioid consumption) among those who consumed opioids. This model produces a multiplicative fixed-effects (ME) output, which represents the ratio in opioid consumption between the groups of interest and can be interpreted as the percent increase or decrease. Q-Q plots of log-transformed opioid consumption during hospitalisation showed adequate approximation of normality (Supplementary Fig. 1). Fixed effects included race, age, sex, insurance, ECIG, hospital characteristics, history of neuropathic pain syndrome, CRPS, chronic pain, fibromyalgia or psychiatric condition, surgical indication, anaesthesia type, multimodal analgesia, complications, LOS, and procedural setting. We included a random effect for hospital and surgeon, as different levels of experience with RA-THA have been reported to affect perioperative outcomes and efficiency.21,22 For our primary outcome, the full models were presented in detail. For the secondary outcomes, only patients who were in the hospital for the timepoint of interest were considered. We reported odds ratios (ORs), MEs, and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Statistical significance was defined as P-value <0.05. To reduce the possibility of false positive results in our primary outcome as a result of three pairwise comparisons, we implemented the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Both adjusted and unadjusted P-values were reported in the tables, but only adjusted P-values were considered. Secondary outcomes and other variables were exploratory and therefore unadjusted P-values were considered. All analyses were conducted using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).

## Discussion

### Key results

In our analysis of 584 578 patients, CA-THA was associated with lower odds of opioid consumption than MA-THA, and RA-THA was associated with higher odds of opioid consumption than CA-THA. The two most important predictors of opioid consumption were number of multimodal analgesia components and anaesthesia type. Among patients who received opioids, CA-THA and RA-THA were associated with a 2% lower total opioid consumption than MA-THA, with discharge year and anaesthesia type as key predictors of total opioid use. The greatest differences were observed on POD 1: CA-THA had significantly lower odds of opioid consumption than MA-THA, and among opioid users, CA-THA and RA-THA were associated with 9% and 6% lower consumption, respectively, compared with MA-THA.

### Interpretation

Whereas other studies have examined the association between technology-assisted THA and opioid use, ours adopted a different analytic approach.5,7,8,23 The first part of our two-step regression analysis examined the odds of consuming opioids in association with surgical modality. We found that CA-THA was associated with lower odds of opioid consumption than MA-THA and RA-THA. The proposed mechanism through which technology-assisted THA might affect opioid requirements is the need for less soft tissue manipulation and the more accurate and efficient acetabular cup placement, which could lead to decreased acute inflammatory response and lower pain.24, 25, 26, 27 Nevertheless, several studies have reported that an entirely opioid-free postoperative course is more related to the structure and implementation of analgesic protocols rather than pain severity alone.28, 29, 30 Thus, it is unlikely that surgical technique alone meaningfully altered the likelihood of remaining opioid-free—particularly because total LOS calculations include day-of-surgery opioid administration, which is often pre-emptive. The differences observed between techniques might reflect residual variation in analgesic pathways that could not be fully captured by the proxy variables available. Considering that CA-THA had almost double the proportion of cases in the outpatient setting compared with RA-THA and MA-THA, it could be that the surgical team and institutional protocols associated with CA-THA are more likely to have implemented an opioid-free enhanced recovery after surgery pathway.

Indeed, the most influential variables affecting opioid-free THA were anaesthesia technique, where neuraxial anaesthesia had the strongest opioid-free effect, and number of multimodal analgesia components, where an increasing number was associated with higher likelihood of receiving any opioids. In contrast, increasing incorporation of multimodal analgesia components was associated with a lower opioid dose among those who consumed opioids. Our lack of knowledge on whether an increasing amount of multimodal analgesia components represents a more comprehensive protocol or a need-based escalation limits the interpretation of this finding. The data pattern perhaps suggests the former, as a more comprehensive analgesic protocol would be more likely to include opioids, but at a lower dose owing to less frequent breakthrough pain and need for rescue medication.31, 32, 33

In contrast, opioid dosage can be influenced significantly more by pain severity.28, 29, 30 Among opioid consumers, we found that technology-assisted THA was associated with lower total opioid consumption. This association confirms the existing but limited data suggesting that RA-THA and CA-THA lead to less opioid consumption than MA-THA in the acute postoperative setting.5,7,8,23 As mentioned above, less soft tissue manipulation and increased accuracy and efficiency in component placement, specifically of the cup, could be the primary drivers behind this association.7,24,27 In theory and based on total knee arthroplasty reports,27 RA-THA and CA-THA might lead to less soft tissue manipulation, as the stereotactic help would allow cup placement to happen with less, but sufficient, visibility. This in turn could lead to a decreased acute inflammatory response that peaks on POD 1 according to a quantitative analysis of tissue injury for minimally invasive THA.34 This could very well explain why the strongest associations between technology use and opioid consumption were observed on POD 1. Unlike the total LOS results, the reduced likelihood of opioid-free status on POD 1 together with lower opioid consumption in technology-assisted THA likely reflects a reduction in early postoperative inflammation and pain. This finding is supported by Piple and colleagues,5 who also described reduction in POD 1 opioid use with technology-assisted THA. Similarly, Buchan and colleagues7 observed no difference in PACU opioid use but observed less opioid consumption with RA-THA on the hospital floor.

Even though results among studies are consistent, the clinical significance of this association is yet to be determined. We observed a 2% reduction in total opioid use and a 6–9% reduction on POD 1 with technology-assisted THA. These findings are similar to Piple and colleagues,5 who reported a 10% reduction on POD 1, and to Oettl and colleagues,23 who found a 0.11 hourly MME reduction with RA-THA. Buchan and colleagues7 reported a 19% reduction with RA-THA relative to MA-THA, but their result was not adjusted for confounding other than opioid tolerance. Based on the available data, a difference likely exists, but it is not clinically meaningful to the extent that it should affect surgical and perioperative decision-making. In fact, our models highlight the significance of opting for neuraxial anaesthesia to completely avoid or reduce opioid use, a fact well established in the perioperative literature.35 Furthermore, the strong association between lower opioid dose and recency of discharge year and the increasing amount of multimodal analgesia components highlight the evolving importance and incorporation of multimodal pain management strategies.16 Taken together, our results indicate that technology-assisted THA may provide small, complementary advantages to current multimodal pain management strategies, which can be thoughtfully incorporated into preoperative discussions with patients.

### Limitations

This study is subject to limitations inherent in its retrospective and observational design, namely causal inference. Although Premier allows for unique population-level conclusions for >25% of US healthcare, selection bias of hospitals opting to be in the database is always a possibility and may be a limiting factor to the generalisability of our results. Moreover, although regular data entry checks are performed,10 entry errors are always possible. Lack of data on history of preoperative opioid use, case complexity, BMI, peripheral nerve block type, and surgical approach (anterior vs posterior) could have affected our results and could pose limitations on our interpretation.36,37 Nonetheless, there are no data that would suggest the distribution of these patients would be different among comparison groups.7 Selection of surgical modality was not randomised, allowing for unknown residual confounding. Nevertheless, the intraoperative complication rate was similar among groups, and surgical time differences were predictable.5 The lack of decision-making information extends to two important variables that affect opioid requirements: anaesthesia choice and multimodal analgesia. To address this, we adjusted for hospital and surgeon, which are the best available proxies for the multidisciplinary team of care as information on the anaesthetist is not available. Still, these two variables represent proxies and not perfect equivalents of institutional and care-team decision-making. Even though our models were adjusted for the number of multimodal analgesia components used, this is only a crude approximation of multimodal use and does not reflect dosing, timing, and adherence to protocols. Finally, patient-reported outcome measures of pain were not available in the dataset, which does not allow for a multidimensional assessment of pain management.

### Conclusions

Among those who consumed opioids, technology-assisted THA was associated with lower opioid consumption than MA-THA, primarily owing to differences observed on POD 1. Although these differences are not clinically significant enough to affect decision-making, patients could be informed before surgery that technology-assisted THA might contribute to an optimal pain management strategy that is primarily driven by the choice of anaesthesia technique and the evolving multimodal analgesia protocols.
